title: Visa Cuts 2,600 Jobs in AI-Driven Restructuring, India Workforce Hit Hard
excerpt: The payments giant is eliminating 7 percent of its global workforce, with technology and product teams bearing the brunt — including at its major engineering hubs in Bengaluru, Mumbai and Chennai.
body:
• Visa is cutting approximately 2,600 positions — 7 percent of its 34,100-strong workforce — primarily in technology and product teams, with significant impact on its India operations
  • CEO Ryan McInerney cited AI as a factor accelerating the restructuring, with product teams shrinking from 10 people to two to four and feature development rising 65 percent
  • India-based employees received layoff emails before dawn on July 29, with senior directors and engineering managers among those affected

Visa has begun cutting approximately 2,600 jobs worldwide, roughly 7 percent of its global workforce, in a restructuring that CEO Ryan McInerney described as essential to capturing a "once-in-a-lifetime inflection point in payments." The layoffs, confirmed on July 29, are hitting the company's technology and product teams hardest — and India's large Visa workforce is feeling the impact acutely.

For some Visa employees in India, the news arrived before their workday began. According to NDTV, layoff emails landed between 4 a.m. and 5 a.m. on July 29. By the time many opened their inboxes, their jobs were gone. One India-based team of 28 reportedly lost 10 members. Senior directors, engineering managers and long-tenured employees were among those affected.

AI Reshapes the Workforce Equation

The cuts are not a response to business weakness. Visa's consumer spending volumes remain resilient, and its transaction-based model insulates it from the credit risk that burdens traditional lenders. This is a restructuring driven by strategic choice, not financial distress.

McInerney made clear in a staff memo, excerpts of which were confirmed to Reuters, that artificial intelligence is central to the shift. "AI is also helping to accelerate this evolution and shape the way work gets done at Visa," he wrote. On the company's earnings call the same day, he went further: "We are going beyond AI assistants. We are able to design, build and ship products with increased velocity."

"We are going beyond AI assistants. We are able to design, build and ship products with increased velocity."

— Ryan McInerney, CEO, Visa

The numbers illustrate the scale of change. Visa's product development teams have been reformed to include two to four people, down from 10, according to American Banker. The company said the leaner structure, combined with AI tooling, has delivered a 65 percent increase in feature development. The restructuring will add $563 million in severance costs.

India Operations Under Pressure

Visa had more than 3,500 employees in India before the cuts, spread across technology and corporate hubs in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Chennai and Hyderabad. The company has not disclosed the India-specific headcount reduction. But former Visa employee Arnab Das highlighted the indiscriminate nature of the cuts on X, noting that his former manager had been laid off despite owning a product end-to-end and receiving strong performance reviews.

Severance packages included notice periods of roughly 15 to 30 days. Some employees reported losing access to company systems within days, with laptops and identification cards returned promptly.

An Industry-Wide Trend

Visa is not alone. Mastercard announced plans earlier this year to trim 4 percent of its global workforce. Fintech firm Block said it would cut nearly half its staff, or 4,000 jobs. Amazon, Cloudflare and Atlassian have also announced significant technology-role reductions, with several explicitly linking cuts to AI-driven efficiency gains.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Visa will reinvest savings into consumer and commercial payments, stablecoins, digital wallet technology and payment orchestration — areas it views as central to the next phase of digital commerce.

What It Means for India's Tech Workforce

For India's technology sector, the Visa layoffs carry broader implications. Global companies have built vast engineering operations in India over the past two decades, employing millions. The question now emerging across boardrooms, as Umesh Kothari of SP Jain School of Global Management told NDTV, is whether AI will reorganise workplaces "from one organised around tasks to one increasingly organised around judgement, problem-solving and decision-making."

For the Indian diaspora in technology roles — both in India and abroad — the message is stark: strong performance alone may no longer guarantee job security in an era where companies are restructuring around AI capabilities rather than headcount.
